channel.title: Sell to the Past
channel.description: I'm a merchant with a time machine. Each episode I take one thing we buy without thinking and try to sell it to people in the past. How many days of work would they pay? And what does it cost us today? 8 minutes, real numbers with sources.
channel.itunes:author: Sell to the Past

item.title: I tried to sell a pane of glass in England in 1780. She had just paid a mason to brick up the window
item.description:
I took a pane of window glass, about ninety-seven dollars, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a widow in Warwickshire in 1447, when a pane cost a glazier fifteen days of work and windows were covered with oiled cloth; to a householder in London in 1755 who paid tax on every window; and to a householder in England in 1780 who bricked up a window to save the tax. The window tax was only repealed in 1851, under pressure from doctors. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what light really costs.
Chapters: 0:00 The pane and the rules 0:35 Warwickshire, 1447: Agnes 3:00 London, 1755: John Hetherington 5:30 England, 1780: Prudence 7:30 Back to today

Backgrounds are AI-generated illustrations made locally; the characters are drawn.

item.title: I tried to sell nails in Scotland in 87 AD. The Romans buried a million instead of selling
item.description:
I took a box of nails, seven dollars and ninety-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a labourer in Virginia in 1796, when the nails for a whole house cost more than a tenth of its value and a law forbade burning houses to get them out; to a nailer in the Black Country in 1842, who struck forty-two thousand hammer blows a day and was paid in goods; and to a Caledonian smith in Scotland in 87 AD, when a retreating Roman legion buried eight hundred and seventy-five thousand nails so they would not become weapons. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a nail is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a mirror to a blind man in 1850. He bought it
item.description:
I took a hand mirror, one dollar and fifty cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a glassmaker on Murano in 1600, who was not allowed to leave the island and whose one mirror was worth thirty years of work; to a noblewoman at Versailles in 1684, when three hundred and fifty-seven mirrors were hung in the Hall of Mirrors; and to a man blind from birth in London in 1850, who wanted a mirror over the hearth to please the friends who could see. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a mirror is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell socks to a stockinger in 1812. He wanted to smash my machine
item.description:
I took a pair of socks, eighteen dollars and ninety-five cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a Roman soldier at the fort of Vindolanda around the year 110, who wrote home asking for socks; to Queen Elizabeth's silk-woman in London in 1583, when a pair of silk stockings cost half a year of a servant's wages; and to a stockinger in Nottingham in 1812, when the new frames cut his wage and breaking a frame was punished by death. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a sock is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell soap in Vienna in 1847. The doctors were offended
item.description:
I took a bar of soap, two dollars and sixty-six cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a soap boiler in London in 1838, when soap was taxed and the excise man locked the pans at night; to a workman's wife in London in 1888, for whom soap was a fixed line in the budget; and to Dr Ignaz Semmelweis at the Vienna General Hospital in 1847, who proved that hand-washing cut maternal mortality from sixteen percent to under two, and the doctors refused to believe it. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what soap is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell oranges on a ship in 1747. A sailor gave a month's wages for eight
item.description:
I took a kilo of oranges, about three dollars and seventy-seven cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to Nell Gwyn, a girl selling oranges at a London theatre in 1665 for sixpence each; to a labourer in London in 1865 who bought an orange for each child's Christmas stocking, two for a penny; and to a sailor on a warship in the English Channel in 1747, when the surgeon James Lind cured scurvy with oranges and lemons, and the fruit ran out. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what an orange is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a carton of milk in New York in 1858. "Pure country milk" killed 8,000 babies a year
item.description:
I took a carton of milk, about a dollar twelve, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a peasant with one cow in England in 1290, where milk had no price at all; to a labourer's wife in London in 1765, who paid an hour and a quarter of work for a watered quart; and to a young mother in Brooklyn in 1858, when distillery swill milk was sold as "pure country milk" and about eight thousand babies a year died from it. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what we buy in a carton.

item.title: I tried to sell a pineapple in London in 1780. She rented it for the evening and gave it back whole
item.description:
I took a pineapple, five dollars and forty-three cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a lord with a hothouse in England in 1760, when one pineapple cost up to eighty pounds; to a building labourer at Covent Garden in 1850, when a street pineapple cost ninepence; and to a merchant's wife in Georgian London, who rented a pineapple for one evening to decorate her table and gave it back whole the next morning. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a pineapple is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a phone with no network in 1772. A sailor paid a month's wages for the clock
item.description:
I took a smartphone, about a hundred dollars, into a time machine. No network and no charger: a clock, a calculator and a torch with one day of battery. I tried to sell it to a sailor on the Atlantic in 1772, when an exact marine clock cost thirty-five years of wages; to a bookkeeping clerk in Chicago in 1903, when a calculating machine cost three months' wages; and to a night watchman in Chicago in 1890, whose battery died in the middle of his shift. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a phone is really worth. Episode twenty.

item.title: I tried to sell a camera in 1870 to a mother who needed one picture. It was worth nothing to her
item.description:
I took a disposable camera, eighteen dollars and ninety-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a messenger in London in 1841, when one portrait cost more than a week of work; to a twelve-year-old girl in a South Carolina cotton mill in 1900, when a one-dollar Brownie cost her three days of work; and to a mother in Ohio in 1870 who needed one picture before the burial, and a travelling tintype photographer gave it to her for five cents in five minutes. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a picture is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell bananas in Bristol in 1945. The rich man offered two weeks' wages, and got none
item.description:
I took a kilo of bananas, about a dollar forty-four, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a costermonger in East London in 1897, who sold two a penny; to a labourer at the Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition in 1876, when one banana cost ten cents and was eaten with a knife and fork; and to a six-year-old girl on the quay in Bristol in December 1945, when the first ship in five years arrived and the government order allowed sales to children only. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a banana is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a roll of toilet paper to a farmer in 1900. He laughed: he had a catalogue
item.description:
I took a roll of toilet paper, forty-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a porter in Pompeii in the year 79, whose bathhouse had one sponge for everyone; to a seamstress in New York in 1857, when Joseph Gayetty sold the first package for half a day of work; and to a farmer in Kansas in 1900, who got a free Sears catalogue every year and hung it on a hook in the outhouse. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what comfort really costs.

item.title: I tried to sell antibiotics in 1946. The buyer could pay, and I refused
item.description:
I took a course of antibiotics, about eleven dollars, into a time machine. I arrived at a ward in Oxford in 1941, where the first patient in the world received penicillin recycled from his own urine; at a munitions worker in Chicago in 1943, when one dose cost 67 hours of work and was rationed to the army; and at a mechanic in Philadelphia in 1946, when the drug already cost 55 cents, and he was allergic. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a medicine is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a can of food to the Franklin expedition. They paid 5 times the price, and got rot
item.description:
I took a can of food, about a dollar thirty-five, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a Royal Navy seaman at Deptford in 1815, when a can of meat cost more than two days of work; to a Union private in Virginia in 1863, who paid the sutler almost two days for a can of condensed milk; and to a sailor on the Franklin expedition in the Arctic in 1845, when the Admiralty paid up to five times the price for its cans, and the officers' cans were the ones that rotted. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what we buy in a can.

item.title: I tried to sell a pen in Cairo in 1834. The buyer paid easily, and couldn't use it
item.description:
I took a ballpoint pen, forty-four cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a junior clerk at the Bank of England in 1810, who went through five quills a day and a tenth of his salary; to a girl in a Birmingham pen-nib factory in 1850, who stamped eighteen thousand nibs a day; and to a labourer in Cairo in 1834, who bought the pen easily and could not write. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a pen is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell chocolate to a soldier who gets it free. He paid three rations for one bar
item.description:
I took a bar of chocolate, about three dollars and thirteen cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a porter in Tenochtitlan in 1520, who carried cacao beans as money and was forbidden to drink them; to a day labourer in Williamsburg in 1770, where a hundred grams cost two hours of work; and to an American private in 1942, who got chocolate for free, but chocolate designed not to melt and to taste only a little better than a boiled potato. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what we buy in chocolate.

item.title: I tried to sell reading glasses to a monk in 1270. He offered a year of work
item.description:
I took a pair of reading glasses, nine dollars and eighty-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell them to a mercer in the Florence market in 1415, where a pair cost a labourer 37 minutes of work; to a farmer's wife in Iowa in 1897 who ordered from the Sears catalogue for half a day of work; and to a monk and scribe in Tuscany in 1270, when spectacles did not yet exist anywhere in the world, and he offered a year of copying. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what glasses are really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a bag of coffee in a camp in 1863. They paid in tobacco
item.description:
I took a bag of coffee, five dollars and fourteen cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a labourer in a London coffeehouse in 1700, where a dish cost a penny and came with a warm room; to a farmer in Prussia in 1777, when King Frederick banned coffee for the people and sent sniffers into the streets; and to a Confederate private in Virginia in 1863, when coffee in the South rose to 196 dollars a pound and soldiers traded tobacco for it between the lines. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what coffee is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a paperback in 1835 to a boy who wasn't allowed to read. He paid in bread
item.description:
I took a paperback, nine dollars and ninety-nine cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a mason in Cambridge in 1400, where one manuscript cost more than a hundred days of work; to a clerk in Mainz in 1455, when Gutenberg sold the first printed Bible for three years of wages; and to Frederick, a twelve-year-old boy held in slavery in Baltimore in 1835, when teaching a slave to read was unlawful, and he paid for letters in bread. Who paid the most, and why, says something about what a book is really worth.

item.title: I tried to sell a box of matches in a trench in 1916. A soldier offered a week's pay
item.description:
I took a box of matches into a time machine. item.title: I tried to sell a T-shirt to a weaver in 1863. He clothed the world and couldn't buy one
item.description:
I took a T-shirt, three dollars and forty-one cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a farm labourer in Rome in 301, when the emperor set a maximum price for a tunic and death for anyone who sold above it; to a spinner in Lancashire in 1745 who earned four pence a day and offered a month of spinning; and to a weaver in Preston in 1863, when the American Civil War stopped the cotton, the mills closed, and families sold their clothes as rags. Who paid the most, and why, says something about the people who make our things.

item.title: I tried to sell a kilo of sugar in 1942. It cost 40 minutes of work, and nobody could buy it
item.description:
I took a kilo of sugar, two dollars and twenty-six cents, into a time machine. I tried to sell it to an apothecary in London in 1319 who sold sugar by the ounce as medicine, to a cane cutter in Jamaica in 1792 who was never paid, and to a mother with a ration book in London in 1942, when sugar was the cheapest in history and nobody could buy more than eight ounces a week. item.title: I tried to sell a bag of ice in 1595. It cost a month of work, and melted by evening
item.description:
I took a bag of ice, about a dollar twenty, into a time machine. item.title: I tried to sell a lantern in a coal mine in 1842. An 8-year-old paid the most for it
item.description:
I took an LED lantern with its batteries into a time machine. I tried to sell it to a hired hand in Babylon 3,800 years ago, where an hour of light at lantern level cost 34 hours of work; to a stocking knitter in England in 1823, who gave two hours of every working day for taxed candles; and to Tommy, an eight-year-old trapper in a coal mine in 1842, who sat twelve hours in the dark because a candle cost 15% of his wage, and a flame could blow up the mine. Who paid the most, and why, says something about who needs light most.

item.title: I tried to sell a supermarket loaf of bread to people in 1795. Here's what they paid
item.description: A standard sliced loaf costs about $2.30 in the US, or 19 minutes of work at the federal minimum wage. In this first episode I take it into a time machine and try to sell it three times: to a farm labourer in England in the hungry summer of 1795, where a loaf cost five hours in the field; to a builder in Rome in 301 AD, where the wheat in a loaf cost two hours but white bread was status; and to a clerk in Paris under siege in 1870, where 300 grams a day were rationed and no money bought more. The best buyer wasn't the richest. All numbers with sources in the description.
